data.Documented value: Care and financial support in ageing families : the changing shape of inequality

Background: Sweden is often seen as a place where older adults and their families are well supported, thanks to comprehensive social policies such as generous pensions, universal healthcare, and publicly funded old age care. These pillars of the Nordic welfare model are designed to ensure equity and relieve families of extensive care and financial responsibilities. However, recent developments such as population ageing, growing socioeconomic inequality, welfare retrenchment, and care marketisation have begun to challenge this model, potentially reshaping how support is provided and received in families. Little is known about how families are adapting to these shifts, especially when it comes to important intergenerational support, such as care for older parents and financial help to adult children and grandchildren. Although prior research has contributed valuable insights, less attention has been paid to the oldest-old, the inclusion of grandchildren, and shifts in multiple care sources over time. Moreover, families may adapt in different ways depending on their gender, social circumstances and socioeconomic position, as access to resources and capacities to provide or seek support vary. Aim: The aim of the thesis was twofold: (1) to deepen understanding of how patterns of care and financial support within ageing families are evolving in the Swedish context, with a focus on intergenerational exchange, and (2) to explore gender and socioeconomic disparities that may both shape and result from these patterns, in light of broader societal change. Data: This thesis addresses the knowledge gaps using nationally representative data from the Swedish Panel Study of Living Conditions of the Oldest Old (SWEOLD), which includes those with the greatest care needs and allows for analysis at the parent-child dyad level, including financial support to grandchildren. Study I: Using data from the sixth wave of SWEOLD from year 2021 and parent- child dyads, findings showed that half of the pairs had some form of support exchange. One-third involved only care from adult child to parent, 14 percent involved only financial support from older parents to adult children and/or grandchildren, and 7 percent engaged in both exchanges. Mothers were more likely to be involved than fathers in any support exchange, even after adjusting for family characteristics and geographical proximity. A higher parental social class belonging increased the likelihood of giving financial support, regardless of the child's social class.

data.Documented value: Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The rise of transnational families has generated new care arrangements in which migrant children use digital technologies to support ageing parents across borders. While the functional role of digital technologies in facilitating remote care is well documented, their relational and culturally embedded dimensions remain less understood. This review synthesises recent evidence on how digital technologies shape transnational caregiving. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: Eight electronic sources were systematically searched for studies on transnational families, ageing, digital technology (including artificial intelligence-AI), and care, published between 2020 and 2025. Eligible studies were extracted, coded, and analysed using thematic analysis. RESULTS: Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis. Five themes were identified: 1) adoption and challenges for transnational ICT-mediated care; 2) ambivalence towards digital intimacy; 3) emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care; 4) cultural norms and moral hierarchies of digital care; 5) structural inequalities in transnational care. Digital technologies both foster connection and amplify separation, serving as symbolic markers of family devotion and tools for managing information across generations. Rather than democratising care, technologies often reinforce existing global North-South, gendered, and class-based inequalities. DISCUSSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Digital technologies both sustain and transform transnational care, yet digitally mediated care remains relational and structurally constrained. Stronger digital inclusion and coordinated cross-border care infrastructures are needed to support ageing transnational families, while avoiding the reproduction of existing social, gendered, and global inequalities, and enabling older adults to age with dignity, connection, and security.

sections.heading: Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families: continued evidence 3
paragraphs: In the realm of transnational families, the integration of digital technologies has significantly transformed the way ageing parents are cared for across borders. This phenomenon, as highlighted in the study "Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families" (S3), underscores the complex interplay between technological advancements and cultural norms. The research reveals that while digital technologies facilitate remote care, they also amplify the physical and emotional distance between generations. This dual effect is particularly evident in the case of migrant children who use digital tools to support their ageing parents, often leading to a new form of emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care. [[S3|The Gerontologist]]

[[S3|The Gerontologist]] The study identifies five key themes that emerge from the analysis of these transnational caregiving practices. Firstly, the adoption and challenges of ICT-mediated care are explored, highlighting the difficulties in maintaining connections and the need for adaptation to local contexts. Secondly, the ambivalence towards digital intimacy is evident, as families grapple with the balance between maintaining a sense of connection and respecting cultural norms. Thirdly, the emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care is discussed, emphasizing the importance of emotional resilience and the strategic concealment of caregiving responsibilities.

Fourthly, cultural norms and moral hierarchies of digital care are examined, revealing how these norms influence the way care is perceived and practiced. Finally, the structural inequalities in transnational care are discussed, underscoring the need for coordinated infrastructures to support ageing transnational families. [[S3|The Gerontologist]] The findings of this study are particularly relevant in understanding the challenges faced by older adults in the context of transnational families. The research highlights the need for stronger digital inclusion and coordinated cross-border care infrastructures to support ageing transnational families.

However, it also cautions against the potential for these technologies to reproduce existing social, gendered, and global inequalities. The study emphasizes the importance of enabling older adults to age with dignity, connection, and security, while avoiding the reproduction of existing social, gendered, and global inequalities. [[S3|The Gerontologist]] The research also underscores the importance of valuing unpaid care labour, as highlighted in the study "The linked lives of Polish worker-carers in the UK and their families in Poland: Making the case for valuing unpaid care labour" (S6). This study provides a qualitative narrative account of Polish worker-carers and their families, exploring the linked lives of these individuals across borders and over the lifecourse.

The research reveals that mobility and fixity can be an opportunity for some individuals to rebalance intergenerational power relations and develop intimacy at a distance, develop non-familial relations of care, or escape toxic relations and remake social reproduction. [[S3|The Gerontologist]]

sections.heading: Policies for Switzerland’s ageing society: continued evidence 4
paragraphs: Switzerland, like many other developed nations, is experiencing an aging population. At the same time, life expectancy is increasing, leading to a significant shift in the demographic landscape. The ratio of retirees to employees is set to soar, with most workers retiring around age 65. This development brings a range of opportunities but will likely weigh on growth in GDP per capita and increase public spending. It may also widen existing inequalities. [[S4|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

The pension system ensures good retirement incomes despite a lack of reforms. However, reforms are urgently needed as the system is under increasing pressure. A range of disincentives and barriers in the labor market and tax system contribute to early retirement and involuntary retirement. Boosting employability at older ages and broadening older workers' options would dampen the economic impact of ageing. [[S4|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

The Swiss health system delivers good outcomes but at a higher cost than other countries, and ageing will only exacerbate the associated pressures. Cost containment and improved coordination are vital. Adjusting the financing of long-term care could improve access and the overall quality of long-term care. [[S4|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

The OECD Economics Department working paper on labour market reform in Japan to cope with a shrinking and ageing population highlights the need for fundamental reform of traditional Japanese labor market practices. A shift to more flexible employment and wage systems based on performance rather than age would enable Japan to better utilise its human capital. Abolishing the right of firms to set mandatory retirement – typically at age 60 – would enable employees to extend their careers and reduce the link between wages and seniority. It would also facilitate a further increase in the pension eligibility age above 65, thereby helping to reduce poverty among the elderly. [[S4|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

Life-long learning is another key element to extending careers. It is also crucial to address a range of issues that discourage the employment of women, namely the lack of work-life balance and shortages of high quality and affordable childcare and long-term care for the elderly. Fighting discrimination and gender stereotypes is also important to allow women to assume greater leadership roles. [[S4|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

Coping with population decline also requires pursuing recent efforts to increase the role of foreign workers in Japan. Breaking down labor market dualism is crucial to expand employment opportunities for women and older people, while reducing income inequality and relative poverty. [[S4|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

sections.heading: The Last-Time Buyer: housing and finance for an ageing society: continued evidence 5
paragraphs: The Baby Boomer generation is retiring and aspirations for later life will prove very different to previous generations. Those retiring at 65 can expect to live for another 23 years, compared with 16 in 1980, and the number of people over 65 is set to rise 52% between 2015 and 2040. It is of course welcome to see people living longer, healthier lives, with more opportunities and plans for retirement. However, this presents increasing challenges in terms of how people manage their finances and for the housing market. [[S5|City Research Online City University London]]

The needs and ambitions of those in later life are becoming more diverse, ranging from household renovations, passing wealth to the next generations and supporting them onto the housing ladder, starting a business venture, contributing to future care costs or seeking more suitable housing for their lifestyle, including downsizing. Much of this will require a boost in their finances, but age has previously acted as a barrier to lending in later life. The financial sector has perhaps been slow to react to the changing needs of the population, but this is rapidly changing. Equity release was the only financial product available, but over the past few years, the choice for over 50s has expanded. [[S5|City Research Online City University London]]

Alongside equity release, there are now Retirement Interest Only (RIO) products with no defined term or minimum equity requirements, along with repayment and fixed-term interest-only mortgages that can be taken out up to the age of 85. This broadens the options available to those in, or about to be in, retirement. Financial advice for older borrowers will remain crucial in driving awareness of the growing range of options. And specialist lenders will play a vital role as they invest time and care in assessing suitability of options to individual circumstances, ensuring lending is responsible with high levels of customer care. [[S5|City Research Online City University London]]

Widening the options for older homeowners requires changing mind-sets further afield than the financial sector. The Government's recent interventions to help first-time buyers have been welcome, but to improve the housing market for the longer-term, there needs to be a refocus towards helping 'last-time buyers', as this report suggests, providing retirees with financial freedoms and creating incentives to downsize, where appropriate, to free up housing stock for younger generations. More detailed and holistic regional plans are also required. [[S5|City Research Online City University London]]

sections.heading: Labour market reform in Japan to cope with a shrinking: continued evidence 7
paragraphs: The OECD Economics Department working paper titled "Labour market reform in Japan to cope with a shrinking and ageing population" emphasizes the necessity of fundamental changes in traditional Japanese labor market practices to address rapid population aging and the era of 100-year lives. The paper suggests a shift towards more flexible employment and wage systems based on performance rather than age, enabling Japan to better utilize its human capital. Abolishing the right of firms to set mandatory retirement at age 60 would allow employees to extend their careers and reduce the link between wages and seniority, facilitating a further increase in the pension eligibility age above 65, thereby helping to reduce poverty among the elderly. Additionally, the paper highlights the importance of life-long learning as a key element in extending careers. [[S7|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

It also addresses issues that discourage the employment of women, such as the lack of work-life balance and shortages of high-quality and affordable childcare and long-term care for the elderly. Fighting discrimination and gender stereotypes is also crucial to allow women to assume greater leadership roles. The OECD Economic Survey of Japan, published in 2019, provides insights into the challenges faced by the Japanese economy and highlights the need for labor market reform to cope with population decline. The survey notes that all countries in Europe are experiencing an aging population, with a decrease in the number of people of working age per retiree. [[S7|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

Health trends among the elderly are mixed, with severe disability declining in some countries but increasing in others, while mild disability and chronic disease are generally increasing. The survey suggests that a better coordination of care across health and social services, as well as across different levels of health care, is crucial. It also recommends measures that reduce the risk of disease and promote the maintenance of function, confidence, and engagement, such as health promotion and disease prevention programs that target the main causes of morbidity and premature mortality, including obesity and hypertension, as well as mental health. Physical exercise and social involvement are also highlighted as particularly important for these activities and interventions. [[S7|OECD Economics Department working papers]]

The period from middle age onwards is particularly important for these activities and interventions. Building adequate systems of long-term care is also crucial, with the OECD Economics Department working paper emphasizing the importance of supporting economic and social integration. The decline in the share of the population of working age that will have to finance the health system can be addressed by measures that enable more older people to remain in the labor force. Policies in support of healthy ageing also need to address the need for the continued social engagement of elderly people. [[S7|OECD Economics Department working papers]]
